messages.content:
When alone with the field marshal the Emperor expressed his dissatisfaction at the slowness of the pursuit and at the mistakes made at Krasnoe and the Berezina, and informed him of his intentions for a future campaign abroad. Kutuzov made no rejoinder or remark. The same submissive, expressionless look with which he had listened to the Emperor's commands on the field of Austerlitz seven years before settled on his face now.

How does Kutuzov react when the Emperor speaks about the pursuit?
He says nothing. He listens with the same quiet, expressionless look he wore at Austerlitz, as if he simply accepts the Emperor's orders.

What does the old count mean when he says Buonaparte has "turned all their heads"?

"All right, all right!" said the old count. "He always flares up! This Buonaparte has turned all their heads; they all think of how he rose from an ensign and became Emperor. Well, well, God grant it," he added, not noticing his visitor's sarcastic smile.
He means that Napoleon's rise from a low army rank to Emperor has filled people with big dreams. Now they all think they could rise as fast as he did.

Why is Pierre so uneasy in this passage?

When the adjutant reminded him of the prisoner, he jerked his head in Pierre's direction with a frown and ordered him to be led away. But where they were to take him Pierre did not know: back to the coach house or to the place of execution his companions had pointed out to him as they crossed the Virgin's Field.
He does not know where the soldiers are taking him. It might be back to the coach house, or it might be the place of execution that his companions pointed out.

Nicholas expected trouble from Ilagin. What does he find instead?

Instead of an enemy, Nicholas found in Ilagin a stately and courteous gentleman who was particularly anxious to make the young count's acquaintance. Having ridden up to Nicholas, Ilagin raised his beaver cap and said he much regretted what had occurred and would have the man punished who had allowed himself to seize a fox hunted by someone else's borzois. He hoped to become better acquainted with the count and invited him to draw his covert.
He finds a polite, dignified gentleman who wants to get to know him. Ilagin apologises, promises to punish the man who seized the fox, and invites Nicholas to hunt his covert.

Read this passage. Why does Prince Andrew visit the Rostovs the next day?

Next day Prince Andrew called at a few houses he had not visited before, and among them at the Rostovs' with whom he had renewed acquaintance at the ball. Apart from considerations of politeness which demanded the call, he wanted to see that original, eager girl who had left such a pleasant impression on his mind, in her own home.
Good manners required him to call. He also wanted to see the eager, original girl he had met at the ball, in her own home.

Five minutes later Daniel and Uvarka were standing in Nicholas' big study. Though Daniel was not a big man, to see him in a room was like seeing a horse or a bear on the floor among the furniture and surroundings of human life. Daniel himself felt this, and as usual stood just inside the door, trying to speak softly and not move, for fear of breaking something in the master's apartment, and he hastened to say all that was necessary so as to get from under that ceiling, out into the open under the sky once more.

How does Daniel behave in the study, and why?
He stands just inside the door, speaks softly and hardly moves. He feels too big for the room and is afraid of breaking something, so he wants to say his piece quickly and get back outdoors.

What trick does Denisov use in his replies to the two generals?

"No, bwother, I have gwown mustaches myself," said Denisov on reading these documents, and he wrote to the German that, despite his heartfelt desire to serve under so valiant and renowned a general, he had to forgo that pleasure because he was already under the command of the Polish general. To the Polish general he replied to the same effect, informing him that he was already under the command of the German.
He politely refuses both. He tells the German general that he already serves under the Polish general, and tells the Polish general that he serves under the German, so he ends up serving neither.

Having uttered these words in an agitated voice the Emperor suddenly turned away as if to hide from Michaud the tears that rose to his eyes, and went to the further end of his study. Having stood there a few moments, he strode back to Michaud and pressed his arm below the elbow with a vigorous movement. The Emperor's mild and handsome face was flushed and his eyes gleamed with resolution and anger.

What signs show how the Emperor is feeling?
He is deeply moved and angry. He turns away to hide his tears, then comes back with a flushed face and eyes bright with resolution and anger.

What happens in the room when the gust of wind comes?

Suddenly a gust of wind beat violently against the casement of the window, from which the double frame had been removed (by order of the prince, one window frame was removed in each room as soon as the larks returned), and, forcing open a loosely closed latch, set the damask curtain flapping and blew out the candle with its chill, snowy draft. Princess Mary shuddered; her nurse, putting down the stocking she was knitting, went to the window and leaning out tried to catch the open casement. The cold wind flapped the ends of her kerchief and her loose locks of gray hair.
The wind forces the latch open, makes the curtain flap and blows out the candle with a cold, snowy draught. Princess Mary shivers, and her nurse goes to the window to catch the casement.

When her hair was done, Natasha, in her short petticoat from under which her dancing shoes showed, and in her mother's dressing jacket, ran up to Sonya, scrutinized her, and then ran to her mother. Turning her mother's head this way and that, she fastened on the cap and, hurriedly kissing her gray hair, ran back to the maids who were turning up the hem of her skirt.

What does this passage show about Natasha as she gets ready?
She is lively and loving. Half dressed, she runs between Sonya, her mother and the maids, fixes her mother's cap and kisses her gray hair.

Why is Boris full of nervous energy that day?

In the higher command there were two sharply defined parties: Kutuzov's party and that of Bennigsen, the chief of staff. Boris belonged to the latter and no one else, while showing servile respect to Kutuzov, could so create an impression that the old fellow was not much good and that Bennigsen managed everything. Now the decisive moment of battle had come when Kutuzov would be destroyed and the power pass to Bennigsen, or even if Kutuzov won the battle it would be felt that everything was done by Bennigsen. In any case many great rewards would have to be given for tomorrow's action, and new men would come to the front. So Boris was full of nervous vivacity all day.
He is on Bennigsen's side, and the next day's battle may bring Bennigsen to power. Rewards will be given and new men will rise, so Boris is tense about who wins.

Lightly swaying on the flexible springs of his carriage and no longer hearing the terrible sounds of the crowd, Rostopchin grew physically calm and, as always happens, as soon as he became physically tranquil his mind devised reasons why he should be mentally tranquil too. The thought which tranquillized Rostopchin was not a new one. Since the world began and men have killed one another no one has ever committed such a crime against his fellow man without comforting himself with this same idea. This idea is le bien public, the hypothetical welfare of other people.

How does Rostopchin calm his mind after leaving the crowd?
Once his body is calm, he finds a comforting idea: the welfare of other people. The writer says everyone who has ever harmed another has comforted himself with this same thought.

What is the old footman trying to show Pierre?

Pierre drove up to the house of the old prince in a most serious mood. The house had escaped the fire; it showed signs of damage but its general aspect was unchanged. The old footman, who met Pierre with a stern face as if wishing to make the visitor feel that the absence of the old prince had not disturbed the order of things in the house, informed him that the princess had gone to her own apartments, and that she received on Sundays.
He wants to show that the old prince's absence has not upset the order of the house. He greets Pierre sternly and says the princess is in her rooms and receives visitors on Sundays.

The princess glanced at her watch and, seeing that she was five minutes late in starting her practice on the clavichord, went into the sitting room with a look of alarm. Between twelve and two o'clock, as the day was mapped out, the prince rested and the princess played the clavichord.

What does the reader learn about daily life in this house?
It runs on a strict timetable. Between twelve and two the prince rests and the princess plays the clavichord, and she looks alarmed when she is five minutes late.

"I am game for his crooked jaw, and for the jaws of Death too, Captain Ahab, if it fairly comes in the way of the business we follow; but I came here to hunt whales, not my commander's vengeance. How many barrels will thy vengeance yield thee even if thou gettest it, Captain Ahab? it will not fetch thee much in our Nantucket market."

What reason does the speaker give for not joining Captain Ahab's revenge?
He says he came to hunt whales for business, not to serve his captain's vengeance. He also points out that revenge will not earn much money in the Nantucket market.

How did the White Whale get his name?

The rest of his body was so streaked, and spotted, and marbled with the same shrouded hue, that, in the end, he had gained his distinctive appellation of the White Whale; a name, indeed, literally justified by his vivid aspect, when seen gliding at high noon through a dark blue sea, leaving a milky-way wake of creamy foam, all spangled with golden gleamings.
His body was streaked and spotted all over with a pale colour. He also looked vivid as he glided through the dark sea at noon, leaving a creamy wake, so the name fitted what people saw.

And thus, while the one ship went cheerily before the breeze, the other stubbornly fought against it; and so the two vessels parted; the crew of the Pequod looking with grave, lingering glances towards the receding Bachelor; but the Bachelor's men never heeding their gaze for the lively revelry they were in. And as Ahab, leaning over the taffrail, eyed the homeward-bound craft, he took from his pocket a small vial of sand, and then looking from the ship to the vial, seemed thereby bringing two remote associations together, for that vial was filled with Nantucket soundings.

What does Ahab do as the two ships part, and what does it connect for him?
He takes out a small vial of sand and looks from the homeward-bound ship to the vial. The sand is from the sea floor near Nantucket, so it links that ship's journey home with his far-off home.

Why is Stubb scolding the cook in this passage?

"And you have once in your life passed a holy church in Cape-Town, where you doubtless overheard a holy parson addressing his hearers as his beloved fellow-creatures, have you, cook! And yet you come here, and tell me such a dreadful lie as you did just now, eh?" said Stubb. "Where do you expect to go to, cook?"
He thinks the cook has just told a dreadful lie. He reminds him that he has heard a parson in church call people his beloved fellow-creatures, then asks where the cook expects to go after lying.

What does Ahab mean when he says, "I'm all aleak myself"?

"And I was not speaking or thinking of that at all. Begone! Let it leak! I'm all aleak myself. Aye! leaks in leaks! not only full of leaky casks, but those leaky casks are in a leaky ship; and that's a far worse plight than the Pequod's, man. Yet I don't stop to plug my leak; for who can find it in the deep-loaded hull; or how hope to plug it, even if found, in this life's howling gale? Starbuck! I'll not have the Burtons hoisted."
He means he is full of troubles and faults himself, so a leaking cask is a small matter. He says he cannot stop to plug his own leak, because he could not even find it.

Even as it was, I thought something of slipping out of the window, but it was the second floor back. I am no coward, but what to make of this head-peddling purple rascal altogether passed my comprehension. Ignorance is the parent of fear, and being completely nonplussed and confounded about the stranger, I confess I was now as much afraid of him as if it was the devil himself who had thus broken into my room at the dead of night. In fact, I was so afraid of him that I was not game enough just then to address him, and demand a satisfactory answer concerning what seemed inexplicable in him.

Why is Ishmael so afraid in the dark room, and what does he say about fear?
He cannot understand the stranger who has come into his room at night. He says ignorance is the parent of fear, meaning that not understanding something makes you more afraid of it.

The English were preceded in the whale fishery by the Hollanders, Zealanders, and Danes; from whom they derived many terms still extant in the fishery; and what is yet more, their fat old fashions, touching plenty to eat and drink. For, as a general thing, the English merchant-ship scrimps her crew; but not so the English whaler. Hence, in the English, this thing of whaling good cheer is not normal and natural, but incidental and particular; and, therefore, must have some special origin, which is here pointed out, and will be still further elucidated.

Why do English whalers feed their crews so well?

Ordinary English merchant ships feed their crews poorly, but whalers do not. The writer says the good cheer is not natural to the English, so it must come from the earlier Dutch, Zealand and Danish whalers.

Why is Ishmael relieved, and what does he decide about Elijah?

I was resolved to satisfy myself whether this ragged Elijah was really dogging us or not, and with that intent crossed the way with Queequeg, and on that side of it retraced our steps. But Elijah passed on, without seeming to notice us. This relieved me; and once more, and finally as it seemed to me, I pronounced him in my heart, a humbug.
He crossed the street to test whether Elijah was following them, and Elijah walked on without noticing. That relieved him, and he decided in his heart that Elijah was a humbug, or fake.

Already several fatalities had attended his chase. But though similar disasters, however little bruited ashore, were by no means unusual in the fishery; yet, in most instances, such seemed the White Whale's infernal aforethought of ferocity, that every dismembering or death that he caused, was not wholly regarded as having been inflicted by an unintelligent agent.

Why did people not treat the White Whale's attacks as an animal's ordinary acts?
Such deaths were common in whaling, but this whale seemed to act with wicked planning. So people did not see the harm he caused as the work of a mindless creature.

What does Queequeg give Ishmael, and how does Ishmael react?

After supper, and another social chat and smoke, we went to our room together. He made me a present of his embalmed head; took out his enormous tobacco wallet, and groping under the tobacco, drew out some thirty dollars in silver; then spreading them on the table, and mechanically dividing them into two equal portions, pushed one of them towards me, and said it was mine. I was going to remonstrate; but he silenced me by pouring them into my trowsers' pockets. I let them stay. He then went about his evening prayers, took out his idol, and removed the paper fireboard. By certain signs and symptoms, I thought he seemed anxious for me to join him; but well knowing what was to follow, I deliberated a moment whether, in case he invited me, I would comply or otherwise.
Queequeg gives him an embalmed head and half of about thirty silver dollars, pouring the coins into Ishmael's pockets. Ishmael starts to object but is silenced, so he lets them stay.

What does the passage tell us about how Estella feels toward Miss Havisham's affection?

We were seated by the fire, as just now described, and Miss Havisham still had Estella's arm drawn through her own, and still clutched Estella's hand in hers, when Estella gradually began to detach herself. She had shown a proud impatience more than once before, and had rather endured that fierce affection than accepted or returned it.
Estella does not welcome it. She has shown proud impatience before, and she has put up with the fierce love rather than accepting or returning it.

After I had turned the worst point of my illness, I began to notice that while all its other features changed, this one consistent feature did not change. Whoever came about me, still settled down into Joe. I opened my eyes in the night, and I saw, in the great chair at the bedside, Joe. I opened my eyes in the day, and, sitting on the window-seat, smoking his pipe in the shaded open window, still I saw Joe. I asked for cooling drink, and the dear hand that gave it me was Joe's. I sank back on my pillow after drinking, and the face that looked so hopefully and tenderly upon me was the face of Joe.

What does Pip notice while he is ill?
Whoever comes near him seems to turn into Joe. Joe sits by his bed day and night, gives him drinks and looks at him with hope and tenderness.

What does Joe mean when he says Pip's sister "comes the Mo-gul" over them?

"Stay a bit. I know what you're a-going to say, Pip; stay a bit! I don't deny that your sister comes the Mo-gul over us, now and again. I don't deny that she do throw us back-falls, and that she do drop down upon us heavy. At such times as when your sister is on the Ram-page, Pip," Joe sank his voice to a whisper and glanced at the door, "candour compels fur to admit that she is a Buster."
He means she bosses them like a tyrant. Joe admits she often comes down on them hard, and he calls her a Buster, though he says it quietly.

She laughed contemptuously, pushed me out, and locked the gate upon me. I went straight to Mr. Pumblechook's, and was immensely relieved to find him not at home. So, leaving word with the shopman on what day I was wanted at Miss Havisham's again, I set off on the four-mile walk to our forge; pondering, as I went along, on all I had seen, and deeply revolving that I was a common labouring-boy; that my hands were coarse; that my boots were thick; that I had fallen into a despicable habit of calling knaves Jacks; that I was much more ignorant than I had considered myself last night, and generally that I was in a low-lived bad way.

How does Pip feel about himself on the walk home from this visit?
He feels ashamed and low. He thinks of himself as a common labouring boy with coarse hands and thick boots, more ignorant than he had believed, and in a bad way.

What does Pip think about the stars outside the kitchen door?

At those times I would get up and look out at the door; for our kitchen door opened at once upon the night, and stood open on summer evenings to air the room. The very stars to which I then raised my eyes, I am afraid I took to be but poor and humble stars for glittering on the rustic objects among which I had passed my life.
He took them to be poor, humble stars, fit only for shining on the plain country things around him. This shows he had started to look down on his simple home.

Why does Jane cry while she studies?

One day I had come to my studies in lower spirits than usual; the ebb was occasioned by a poignantly felt disappointment. Hannah had told me in the morning there was a letter for me, and when I went down to take it, almost certain that the long-looked for tidings were vouchsafed me at last, I found only an unimportant note from Mr. Briggs on business. The bitter check had wrung from me some tears; and now, as I sat poring over the crabbed characters and flourishing tropes of an Indian scribe, my eyes filled again.
She had hoped a letter would bring news she had waited a long time for. It was only an unimportant business note from Mr. Briggs, and the disappointment made her cry.

"If it were not such a very wild night," he said, "I would send Hannah down to keep you company: you look too desperately miserable to be left alone. But Hannah, poor woman! could not stride the drifts so well as I: her legs are not quite so long: so I must e'en leave you to your sorrows. Good-night."

Why does he not send Hannah to keep her company?
He would like her to have company on such a wild night. But Hannah cannot stride through the snowdrifts as well as he can, so he says good night and leaves her alone with her sorrows.

What does the speaker tell Jane to do whenever she imagines Mr. Rochester thinks well of her?

"Whenever, in future, you should chance to fancy Mr. Rochester thinks well of you, take out these two pictures and compare them: say, 'Mr. Rochester might probably win that noble lady's love, if he chose to strive for it; is it likely he would waste a serious thought on this indigent and insignificant plebeian?'"
He tells her to compare the two pictures and remind herself that he could win a noble lady's love. So he would hardly think seriously about a poor, unimportant girl like her.

I did not need to be guided to the well-known room, to which I had so often been summoned for chastisement or reprimand in former days. I hastened before Bessie; I softly opened the door: a shaded light stood on the table, for it was now getting dark. There was the great four-post bed with amber hangings as of old; there the toilet-table, the armchair, and the footstool, at which I had a hundred times been sentenced to kneel, to ask pardon for offences by me uncommitted. I looked into a certain corner near, half-expecting to see the slim outline of a once dreaded switch which used to lurk there, waiting to leap out imp-like and lace my quivering palm or shrinking neck. I approached the bed; I opened the curtains and leant over the high-piled pillows.

What memories come back to Jane in this room?

She remembers being sent there to be punished or scolded. She recalls kneeling on the footstool to ask pardon for faults she had not committed, and she even looks for the switch that used to wait in the corner.

Why do the men want horses ready, and why must the earth be destroyed between sunrise and sunset?

To-day Harker is out following up his clue, and Art and Quincey are looking after horses. Godalming thinks that it will be well to have horses always in readiness, for when we get the information which we seek there will be no time to lose. We must sterilise all the imported earth between sunrise and sunset; we shall thus catch the Count at his weakest, and without a refuge to fly to. Van Helsing is off to the British Museum looking up some authorities on ancient medicine. The old physicians took account of things which their followers do not accept, and the Professor is searching for witch and demon cures which may be useful to us later.
Horses must be ready because, once they know where to go, there will be no time to lose. Destroying the earth in daylight will catch the Count at his weakest, with no safe place to hide.

"Look here, old fellow," said Morris, "it is a capital idea to have all ready in case we want to go horsebacking; but don't you think that one of your snappy carriages with its heraldic adornments in a byway of Walworth or Mile End would attract too much attention for our purposes? It seems to me that we ought to take cabs when we go south or east; and even leave them somewhere near the neighbourhood we are going to."

What worry does Morris raise about the carriages?
He thinks a smart carriage with heraldic decorations would attract too much attention in poor districts like Walworth or Mile End. He suggests taking cabs and leaving them near the place.

How does Lucy look at the end of this passage, and what do the men feel?

There, in the coffin lay no longer the foul Thing that we had so dreaded and grown to hate that the work of her destruction was yielded as a privilege to the one best entitled to it, but Lucy as we had seen her in her life, with her face of unequalled sweetness and purity. True that there were there, as we had seen them in life, the traces of care and pain and waste; but these were all dear to us, for they marked her truth to what we knew. One and all we felt that the holy calm that lay like sunshine over the wasted face and form was only an earthly token and symbol of the calm that was to reign for ever.
She looks as she did in life, sweet and pure, with only faint marks of care and pain. The men feel a holy calm and take it as a sign of the calm that will last for ever.

"One day, O Brahmana, Ruru entered an extensive forest. And there he saw an old serpent of the Dundubha species lying stretched on the ground. And Ruru thereupon lifted up in anger his staff, even like to the staff of Death, for the purpose of killing it. Then the Dundubha, addressing Ruru, said, 'I have done thee no harm, O Brahmana! Then wherefore wilt thou slay me in anger?'"

What does the serpent say to Ruru, and why?
The old serpent says it has done Ruru no harm and asks why he wants to kill it in anger. Ruru had lifted his staff to strike it.

Why does Yudhishthira say it is not strange that Virata's son won?

Vaisampayana continued, "Meanwhile, the swift-footed messengers despatched by Uttara, having reached Virata's city, gave tidings of the victory. And the minister-in-chief then informed the king of everything, viz., the great victory that had been won, the defeat of the Kurus, and the expected arrival of Uttara. And he said, 'All the kine have been brought back, the Kurus have been defeated, and Uttara, that slayer of foes, is well with his car-driver.' Then Yudhishthira said, 'By good luck it is that the kine have been recovered and the Kurus routed. I do not, however, regard it strange that thy son should have vanquished the Kurus, for his victory is assured that hath Vrihannala for his charioteer.'"
Because Uttara's charioteer was Vrihannala. Yudhishthira means that, with such a charioteer, the victory was certain.

The science fair was next morning, the school hall had no power, and Jeevan's solar oven still needed three more hours. He had built it at home from a shoebox and foil, working by lantern. At four, Mrs Elizabeth Mathew walked past his table in the dim hall and stopped. "Oh, Jeevan, you've actually made something? Well. Wonders." She laughed kindly and moved on. He looked at the shoebox. For two weeks he had been sure it was good. Now he wasn't. Maybe she was right, and it would fail in front of everyone tomorrow, and they would all see. By five he had packed it into his bag. When the fair list went up, his name wasn't on it. "I didn't finish," he told his friend Asif, which was not true.

Why does Jeevan tell Asif that he did not finish?
After the teacher's remark he began to doubt his oven and gave up before the fair. He did not want to admit that, so he said he had not finished, which was untrue.

Recess was only ten minutes today because of the assembly, and Akash was picking the kho-kho team fast. "You, you, you." He skipped right past Tsering, the new boy whose family had come from Darjeeling. "Not him, he talks funny." A few kids laughed. Aparna felt her face go hot. Tsering looked down at his shoes. There were only seven minutes left. Aparna could have just played. Instead she said loudly, "That's not fair. He runs faster than you, Akash. And how he talks has nothing to do with kho-kho." Akash rolled his eyes. "Fine, take him then." Aparna pulled Tsering onto her side. He tagged three people before the bell. On the way back in, he walked next to her.

What does Aparna do when Akash leaves Tsering out, and what happens next?

She speaks up and says it is unfair, because Tsering runs faster and his way of talking has nothing to do with the game. Akash lets him join her team, and Tsering tags three players and walks beside her afterwards.

How did Omkar feel about the party in the end?

Tushar's birthday party in their Pune society hall lasted the whole afternoon. There was musical chairs, a magician who forgot his tricks, samosas, a long wait for Tushar's cousins, and a treasure hunt Omkar didn't win. Then the cake came out with a sparkler fizzing on top, the lights went off, and Omkar, nine, screamed with joy along with everyone else. At the very end, as he was leaving, his return-gift balloon slipped from his hand and floated up to the ceiling fan. It popped. In the car Mummy asked, "How was the party?" "The sparkler was the best thing ever," Omkar said. Then his face crumpled. "But my balloon popped. It was kind of a sad party." Mummy thought of four hours of photos on her phone and said nothing.
He enjoyed it, especially the sparkler, but he felt sad when his balloon popped. That small loss made the whole party seem a little sad to him, even after hours of fun.

It was raining hard on Kalyani's first day at the new playgroup, so all the children were squeezed onto the veranda, wet shoes everywhere. Kalyani, five, stood by the door holding her mother's hand. A boy was sitting on the step with a toy lorry. Kalyani let go of the hand and walked over. "Hello." The boy looked up. "Hello." "I ate idli for breakfast. With chutney." "I ate bread." Kalyani sat down next to him. "What's your name?" "Karthik." "I'm Kalyani." Karthik pushed the lorry toward her. She pushed it back.

How do the two children become friends?
Kalyani, new and a little nervous, walks over on her own and says hello. They talk about breakfast, share their names, and the boy pushes his toy lorry to her to play.

Why did Sachin say that cricket was boring?

Saturday. Sachin's diary. The team list went up. I wasn't on it. Dolma asked if I was okay and I said, "Whatever, cricket's boring anyway." I even laughed. Then I went home and lay on my bed for two hours. The truth is I practised every evening for a month. If I say I don't care, then it doesn't look like I lost. That's the idea, anyway. But it doesn't make the heavy feeling go away. Dolma messaged later: "You're allowed to be upset, you know." I didn't reply. I'll maybe reply tomorrow. Or talk to Coach about what I can work on.
He was hurt about missing the team after a month of daily practice. Saying he did not care was his way of making it look as if he had not lost.

'Baba, why is my bicycle still in the balcony?' Bidisha's father looked up from the paper. 'Where else would it go?' 'I left for Bengaluru two years ago.' 'You might come back one day and want to ride.' Pranav, Bidisha's husband, caught her eye. 'And the mosquito net on my old bed?' 'It's monsoon. You never know.' 'Baba, I visit twice a year.' Her father folded the newspaper slowly. 'Your mother puts out your plate every Sunday. Out of habit.' He looked at the door. 'We wait. It's what parents do.' Bidisha's eyes filled. She sat beside him. 'I'll come for Durga Puja, Baba. And I'll call on Sundays when Ma puts out the plate.' Her father patted her hand and didn't say anything for a while.

What does Bidisha's father mean by "We wait. It's what parents do"?
He means her parents keep her things ready and hope she will visit, like her bicycle, the mosquito net and the plate her mother sets out each Sunday. It shows how much they miss her.

What did Zainab Ma'am notice about Pradeep, and what changed?

Week one. Every day Pradeep's tiffin held sweet biscuits and a packet of jelly sweets. By eleven he was drumming on the desk and chatting nonstop. By twelve he was yawning, head on his arms, snapping at anyone who spoke to him. Zainab Ma'am noticed the pattern. Week two. She mentioned it gently to his father at pickup, without blame. "Nothing needs banning," she said. "Maybe something filling alongside?" His father nodded; he had noticed the evening grumps too. Week four. Pradeep's tiffin now held a paratha with paneer, some fruit and one biscuit as a treat. At twelve he was still upright, finishing his sums, and he laughed when he got one wrong instead of throwing his pencil.
He was lively after sweets but tired and snappy by noon. She told his father gently, he added a filling meal to the tiffin, and Pradeep stayed steady and cheerful.

For peace week, Reena's class in Guwahati painted posters. Reena drew a white dove carrying an olive twig and used soft blues so the page felt calm. Where she lives, calling someone an owl, or ullu, means they are silly. Lalremsiami's storybooks treat the owl as wise, so the same bird means different things in different places.

What does the reader learn about how Dadi talks with Ramesh?

He told the possum story as if he had seen it, but he was asleep in the tent. He starts to wonder whether he really saw any of it, since his only photo shows crumbs.

Why did Kamal not hear his mother call him for lunch?

He heard Hemant's mother say they had moved three times in two years, and he realised the laugh on the first day was nerves. Looking again, he saw a kind, slightly loud boy, not a show-off.

What does the passage show about Anatole's character?

She hurries away, then comes back looking frightened but determined. She unfolds a kerchief and quickly hands him a white twenty-five-ruble note.

She feels she must see the man lying there, though he looks horribly unlike a man. She passes the frightened valet and finds Prince Andrew looking just as she had always known him.

He feels unbearable pain at every jolt and becomes feverish and delirious. In his visions he sees his father, wife, sister and future son, the little Napoleon, and the lofty sky.

What happens to Pierre after he is freed?

What does the narrator notice from the window of the inn?

She says she is tired of the life she has led, which has few charms, and is willing to change it. She refuses to be blamed for a fatal step and says they will never understand each other.

He repeats "I love her" hundreds of times, copying Miss Havisham's words. He feels grateful that she is meant for him, but he wonders when she will begin to care for him.

'Last time Papa did all this for you.' 'That's why I'm doing it now.' She uncapped her pen. 'I also booked my own eye test, and I set up my phone bill to pay itself. Small things.' 'Since when are you so grown up?' 'I'm not. I still called Mummy yesterday to ask how long to boil eggs.' She grinned. 'But I read somewhere you don't wake up an adult one day. You just do the next thing yourself.' Kishore leaned back. 'Fine. But if you write your birth date in the wrong box, I'm laughing.' 'Deal.'
She wants to do things on her own now, instead of letting her father or brother do them. She says she handles small tasks herself, and that people grow up by doing the next thing themselves.

Chinmay, you asked how I run the lab. Thomas here. When I started, I said things like "Clean the bench" and "Redo the samples," and people did it, but half of them looked at the floor. One day a junior said quietly, "I don't know why we redo them." I was embarrassed. That was fair. Now I say, "Please redo the samples today, because the last batch was contaminated, and I need clean results by Friday for the report." Same request, but with the reason and the result. The mood changed. People started asking smart questions and catching mistakes I hadn't seen. Commands can get things done for a while, but explanations get you people who care.

What did Thomas change about how he gives instructions, and what was the result?
He began to give the reason and the deadline along with each request, instead of bare commands. People then asked smart questions, caught mistakes and cared more about the work.

How did Kamal Dada's father help him when he broke his arm?

Sumit, beta, stop scowling at that cast. Come sit with your Kamal Dada. When I was nine, in our village, I climbed the tallest mango tree and fell straight out of it. Snap went my arm. I screamed so loud the goats ran. I was frightened, and then I was angry, because it was kabaddi season and I was the best raider. I thought my arm would never be the same. My father sat with me that night. He didn't say 'stop crying'. He told me straight: 'Six weeks in the cast, then it will be weak, then it will get strong.' And every week he gave me a small job: carry the milk tin with my good hand, then squeeze a rubber ball. By the next season, I was raiding again. So, one week at a time, eh?
He did not tell him to stop crying. He explained plainly how the recovery would go and gave him a small job each week, like carrying the milk tin and squeezing a rubber ball.

June: Vijay moved to Pune for his first job; Amandeep stayed in Chandigarh for his master's. They promised to call every week. By August, they hadn't spoken in five weeks. September: Vijay forgot Amandeep's birthday. He saw it the next morning on social media and felt terrible. He called at lunch. Amandeep answered, a little cool. "Busy life, huh?" "No excuse. I'm sorry. Can we fix the rhythm? Calls don't work for us." They tried something smaller: a voice note every Sunday, even thirty seconds, about the best and worst thing of the week. December: Vijay had nineteen voice notes saved. He knew about Amandeep's new flatmate, his bad professor, his sister's engagement. When Vijay visited home for New Year, they talked till two in the morning like nothing had changed.

How do Vijay and Amandeep keep their friendship going?

When weekly calls failed, they switched to a Sunday voice note about the best and worst thing of the week, even if only thirty seconds long. By December Vijay knew what was going on in Amandeep's life.

What does Trisha mean by "Different rooms, same Trisha"?

In my village near Ranchi, I'm Trisha-didi: the one who carries water, respects every elder and speaks Kurukh with my grandmother. In Delhi, where I study now, I'm Trisha from the college drama club, loud, in jeans, arguing about plays at midnight. For my first year I felt like a fake in both places. When I went home, my cousin Kamal teased me: "City girl!" When I came back, my friends laughed at my accent. I cried about it once, on the train. Then my drama teacher said something that stuck: "An actor isn't lying when she changes her voice. She's using more of herself." Now I think of it that way. Different rooms, same Trisha.

She means she is one person who acts differently in different places, like the village girl and the college drama club member. Her teacher helped her see that changing is not being fake, but using more of herself.

Tomas had finished a general science degree in Prague and still felt he couldn't do anything anyone would pay for. So he joined a twelve-week coding course in a cramped office above a bakery. The first week he wanted to quit; everyone else seemed to type faster. Leila, the course mentor, noticed him staring at an error for twenty minutes. "Read the message out loud," she said. He did, and saw the missing bracket. "Now fix one thing at a time." Each evening he rebuilt the day's exercise from scratch without looking. By week eight he built a small booking page for his aunt's hair salon. It was ugly, but it worked. When she used it to take her first appointment, Tomas stared at the screen, grinning.

What helped Tomas get better at coding?
Leila told him to read error messages aloud and fix one thing at a time. He also rebuilt each day's exercise from scratch every evening, and by week eight he had made a booking page that worked.

What does Kamal do to help Rukmini, and why does it work?

Rukmini was always the first to arrive at the college canteen in Andheri and the last to leave, arguing about films. So Kamal noticed when she disappeared. She had missed four accounts lectures in a row. When he texted, she sent jokes but ignored questions. When a classmate mentioned the ATKT form for the failed accounts paper, she suddenly remembered she had to "rush home". Kamal didn't want to lecture her; everyone else already had. On Saturday he messaged: "Chai at the station stall at 5? I'll bring the ATKT form. We'll just fill in your name. Nothing else." She came, late and quiet. They filled in her name and roll number. Then they talked about a film for an hour. On Monday she was back in the accounts lecture, sitting next to him.
He does not lecture her. He invites her for chai and offers to fill in only her name on the form, so the task feels small. She comes, they fill it in, and she returns to class.

Tuesday. Gurpreet finally told Papa about the boy who kept tearing her notebooks. Harish went red and grabbed the car keys. "I'll go to that school right now!" Gurpreet grabbed his arm. "Please, Papa, don't! Everyone will know!" Harish stopped. He sat back down. "You're right. Tell me everything first." He listened, then said, "Thank you for trusting me." Wednesday. They made a list together of dates and torn pages. Harish emailed the class teacher and asked for a meeting with Gurpreet present. The next Monday. The boy had been moved to another section. That evening Gurpreet told Papa about a small fight with her friend, without being asked.

How did Harish respond after Gurpreet asked him not to rush to the school?
He stopped and sat down, then listened to her whole story. He thanked her for trusting him, made a list of dates with her, and asked for a meeting with her present.

How does Tanvir Ma'am help Sudha learn?

In her second week at the marketing firm, Sudha sat beside Tanvir Kaur for forty minutes over a spreadsheet. "Try it first, then I'll show you," Tanvir Ma'am said. It was the first real task Sudha had been given: the client's monthly report. When the numbers came out wrong, Tanvir Ma'am did not sigh. She circled one cell and asked, "What do you think happened here?" Sudha found the slip herself. On her last Friday, Sudha asked shyly for a reference and for feedback, and Tanvir Ma'am listed two things to work on. That evening Sudha texted a friend that she wanted to be exactly like her manager, then paused and wrote her own plan: message every month, prepare for the other interview, finish her own project.
She lets Sudha try the task first and, when the numbers are wrong, asks what she thinks happened instead of sighing. She also gives honest feedback, listing two things to work on.

I'm Sabina, and three interviews had ended with the same polite line about my missing experience. Then Bhupen read my portfolio and said, "Start on the fifteenth." I have never forgotten that. So when I found that the pricing sheet Bhupen had sent to two clients used the old tax rate, my chest went tight. It felt ungrateful to point at a mistake made by the person who took a chance on me. I waited a day. Then I walked over with the sheet in hand and said, "I think this rate is outdated. Could we check?" Bhupen looked, groaned, and said, "Thank you. Send me the corrected version and I will call both clients." I understood then that being honest was one of the ways of saying thanks.

Why does Sabina hesitate to point out the mistake, and what does she do in the end?
Bhupen gave her a chance when others did not, so correcting him feels ungrateful. After a day she calmly shows him the sheet and asks if the rate is outdated, and he thanks her.

How did Sarita handle the hurtful remark, and what did Pankaj learn?

You want to know when I knew? It wasn't some big romantic moment. I'm Pankaj, by the way. My wife Sarita and I were fighting about her job offer in Hyderabad, and I said something mean: that she only cared about her career. In my family, a line like that got you three days of silence. Sarita just said, "That hurt. Can you tell me what's under it?" And what was under it was fear, that I'd be the one left behind. She heard that without making me pay for it. We moved together in the end, on a plan we both chose. Now when I'm scared, I say so early. It's easier to be brave next to someone who stays.
She said it hurt and asked what was under it. Pankaj saw that it was fear of being left behind, and she heard it without making him pay. Now he says when he is scared, early.
